opus-5.5.text:
I like to frame this with the history of astronomy, because I think it maps onto AI surprisingly well. You have three stages: Tycho Brahe, Kepler, and Newton. Tycho collected a huge amount of very precise observational data. Kepler looked at that data and found empirical regularities: elliptical orbits, the area law, the relation between period and orbital radius. Those were beautiful patterns, but they were still phenomenological. Then Newton came along and explained *why* those patterns hold, with gravity and the laws of motion. That's when you have a fundamental theory.

If I'm honest, I think AI research today is somewhere between Tycho and Kepler. We've been in the Tycho stage for a long time. We train enormous models, run lots of experiments, and collect lots of observations about what works and what doesn't. A lot of this is engineering intuition and trial and error.

In the past few years we've started to see some Kepler-like results. Scaling laws are the most famous example: loss goes down as a power law in compute, data, and parameters. That's a clean empirical regularity, very much like Kepler's third law. There are also phenomena like grokking, emergent abilities, and various observations from mechanistic interpretability about how features and circuits form. These are patterns we can measure and sometimes predict.

But we don't really have a Newton yet. We don't have a deep, unified theory that tells us *why* scaling laws have the exponents they do, or *why* certain representations emerge, from first principles. We have some toy models and partial explanations, but nothing like a set of fundamental laws of intelligence or learning.

This is what motivates what I call the "physics of AI" approach. Instead of trying to jump straight to a grand theory, which is very hard for such complex systems, we should do what physicists do. Build simple, controlled toy models, observe phenomena carefully, find the regularities, and gradually build up explanations. Physics didn't start with quantum field theory. It started with people rolling balls down inclined planes.

There's also a twist that I find exciting. AI is not only the *object* of this kind of science. It may also become a *tool* for it. Could AI systems help us do the Kepler step, or even the Newton step, for science in general? Much of my work on interpretable models, like KANs, is motivated by that question. If a model can not only fit data but also give us something symbolic and understandable, then it could help scientists move from observations to laws. Right now most neural networks are very good Tychos. They absorb data and make predictions. Some are starting to behave a little like Kepler. Getting to Newton, where the system finds the underlying principle and expresses it in a way humans can understand and build on, is still an open challenge. And I think it's one of the most important ones.

fable-5.1.text:
I like to think about this using the history of physics as a map. If you look at how we got to Newton's laws, there's a clear progression. First you have Tycho Brahe, who spent decades just collecting data, very precise observations of planetary positions. Then you have Kepler, who stared at that data and found patterns, the elliptical orbits, the three laws. And then finally Newton, who asked why those patterns exist and came up with gravitation, a single principle that explains Kepler's laws and much more.

So you have three stages: observation, phenomenology, and theory. And I think AI research right now is mostly somewhere between the first and second stage. We are extremely good at the Tycho Brahe part. We run massive experiments, we train huge models, we collect loss curves, benchmark numbers, all of this data. And we are starting to be decent at the Kepler part. Scaling laws are a good example. People noticed that loss follows a power law in compute and data, and that's a genuine empirical regularity, something you can fit and predict with. Grokking, emergence, phase transitions in training, these are all Kepler-type findings. We see the pattern, we can describe it mathematically.

But we are quite far from the Newton stage. We don't really have a first-principles theory that tells us why the exponent in a scaling law takes a particular value, or why a transformer should be the right architecture, or what the model is actually computing inside. Most of what we call theory in deep learning is either very idealized, like infinite-width limits, or it's post hoc explanation of something we already observed empirically.

And honestly I think this is fine, maybe even necessary. Physics didn't skip stages either. Kepler needed Brahe's data, and Newton needed Kepler's laws to have something to explain. What I try to do in my own work, whether it's mechanistic interpretability or things like KAN, is to push toward that second and third stage. Take a small, controlled system, look very carefully at what the network learns, and try to extract a principle from it rather than just another benchmark number. Because I believe the field will eventually need its own Newton moment, and that only comes if some of us treat deep learning as a natural science rather than purely as engineering.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re still largely in the stage of collecting observations, although we’re starting to find some regularities. We train models, change their size or their data, and observe what happens. Scaling laws are a good example of turning those observations into a quantitative relationship. But a relationship that predicts performance is not yet a fundamental explanation of why learning works.

You could compare this to the distinction between Kepler’s laws and Newton’s laws. Kepler described regularities in planetary motion; Newton provided a framework that explained them and connected them to other phenomena. In AI, we have some things that look like Kepler’s laws, but I don’t think we have an equivalent of Newton’s framework yet.

My intuition is that studying simpler, controlled systems will be important. If we can understand how a small network learns a particular structure, we can formulate a hypothesis and test whether it also applies to larger networks. The challenge is to find simplifications that preserve the phenomenon we actually want to explain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI is still largely in the stage of collecting observations and finding empirical regularities. We have very powerful systems, and we know many recipes that work, but our ability to explain why they work—and predict when they will fail—is much less developed.

You can think of the history of physics: careful observations came first, then people found patterns, and eventually those patterns were connected by a small set of principles. In AI, scaling laws are one example of an empirical regularity. They tell us something useful about how performance changes with resources, but they don’t yet give us a complete theory of learning or intelligence.

So I think the opportunity is to move between experiments and theory: study systems simple enough that we can understand them, identify mechanisms, and then test whether those mechanisms survive at larger scales. The challenge is figuring out which details are incidental and which are essential. We have a lot of observations now. Turning those into a compact, predictive understanding is still an open problem.
